answer: Our building is full of friendly people, but one neighbour really stands out. I would like to talk about an elderly gentleman who lives in the flat opposite ours on the third floor and has been there for as long as we have, which is well over a decade now, so I have practically grown up around him. Despite the age gap, we have always got on remarkably well. He is the sort of neighbour everyone wishes they had: friendly, respectful and never [[intrusive]]. He is a retired government officer who lives alone now that his children have moved abroad, so he enjoys a bit of company. He keeps an eye on our flat when we visit my grandparents in the village, and in return we help him with anything that requires climbing a ladder or heavy lifting, like carrying his shopping up the stairs. What I like most is his endless supply of fascinating stories from his younger years, which are genuinely [[captivating]]. He is also incredibly [[considerate]], always mindful of noise and careful never to overstep. On Friday evenings he sometimes invites me in for tea, and we end up discussing cricket and politics for hours. I think good neighbours are a kind of quiet blessing that people underestimate until they lose them. Over the years he has become almost like extended family, and the building would feel noticeably [[emptier]] without him. Honestly, his presence is a big part of what makes our neighbourhood feel like home.

followUps.q: Do you think it is important to have good neighbours?
followUps.answer: Absolutely. Neighbours are often the first people who can help in an emergency, long before family arrives. Living near people you trust also gives you real [[peace of mind]] every day.

followUps.q: Do you know most of your neighbours well?
followUps.answer: Most of the ones in our building, yes. We greet each other on the stairs and exchange food during Eid, although I know the newer families less well than those who have been here for years.
